headline: Scientists look into baby whale deaths in Argentina

sources.title: Scientists search for answers as baby whales wash up dead in Argentina (AP)
Bacteria suspected in deaths of hundreds of baby whales off Argentina (AFP, via Phys.org)
Investigan la causa de la inusual mortandad de ballenatos en Península Valdés: una bacteria es una de las hipótesis (Infobae)

chunks.text: Scientists are {{looking into}} why baby whales are {{dying off}} in large numbers in 2026. Since June 2026, dead southern right whale [[calves]] have been {{washing up}} on beaches around a peninsula in southern Argentina. The area is a major [[breeding ground]] for the [[species]]. [[Residents]] have reported hundreds of dead calves. Researchers have not given an official [[death toll]]. They say it will be clearer after the season ends in late November.

verbs.correct: To study something to learn the facts
verbs.wrong: To keep young animals safe and fed
verbs.why: The police are looking into the break-in at the school. My bank is looking into the strange charge on my card. Scientists in Argentina are looking into why so many baby whales have died in 2026.

chunks.text: In the 19th and 20th centuries, [[whalers]] nearly {{wiped out}} southern right whales. The species has been protected since 1935 and has slowly {{bounced back}}. Every year, the whales return to the peninsula's [[sheltered waters]] to [[give birth]] and [[nurse]] their young. The 2026 count found nearly 400 calves, down from about 800 in 2025. In 2012, a [[record]] 113 dead calves were found. A whale group says the 2026 number could be higher.

verbs.correct: To destroy or kill all of something
verbs.wrong: To count all the animals in an area
verbs.why: A disease wiped out most of the frogs in the lake. The flood wiped out the farmer's whole crop. In the 19th and 20th centuries, whalers nearly wiped out southern right whales.

verbs.correct: To become strong again after trouble
verbs.wrong: To hide in a place hunters cannot reach
verbs.why: The town bounced back quickly after the fire. Sales bounced back in the spring. Southern right whales have slowly bounced back since they were protected in 1935.

chunks.text: On October 2, the scientists described their [[leading theory]]. It involves a bird called the kelp gull. The gulls {{go after}} whales that {{come up}} to breathe, and they eat bits of their skin. Adult whales have learned to keep their backs under the water. Calves have not, so they get [[wounds]]. Scientists think bacteria from the sea enter the calves through these wounds. Bacteria have already {{turned up}} in some [[tissue samples]].

verbs.correct: To attack or chase an animal
verbs.wrong: To build nests on a beach
verbs.why: Our cat likes to go after birds in the yard. The dog went after a rabbit in the field. Kelp gulls go after southern right whales when they rise to breathe.

verbs.correct: To rise to the top of the water
verbs.wrong: To swim next to its mother
verbs.why: The diver came up for air after a minute. We watched a seal come up near the boat. The gulls attack whales that come up to breathe.
My lost keys turned up in my coat pocket. New problems turned up during the safety check. Bacteria have already turned up in some tissue samples from the dead calves.

chunks.text: The team's leader, a veterinarian from a US university, said changes in the ocean may [[play a part]]. Warmer water, possibly linked to [[climate change]], could make the bacteria too strong for the calves to {{fight off}}. Another researcher in Argentina said the cause seems natural. Still, he cannot fully {{rule out}} a human role. Scientists warn that repeated deaths on this scale could {{set back}} the species' [[recovery]]. The team wants to {{figure out}} what [[triggered]] the 2026 deaths.

mainIdea.s: In 2026, far more whale calves than usual have died near a peninsula in Argentina. Researchers suspect sea bacteria that enter through wounds made by gulls.
mainIdea.why: Dead calves have been washing up since June. The leading theory is that bacteria enter wounds made by kelp gulls, and warmer water may help.

mainIdea.s: Scientists have confirmed that warm ocean water is now killing young whales in southern Argentina. They say bacteria and gulls have nothing to do with the deaths.
mainIdea.why: Close, but nothing is confirmed yet. Bacteria in gull wounds are the main suspect, and warmer water may only make those bacteria stronger.

mainIdea.s: A large group of adult whales got stuck on a beach in Argentina in March. Local people and rescue teams worked for hours to return most of them to the sea.
mainIdea.why: No whales were rescued. Scientists are trying to learn why so many baby whales have died in 2026.

lines.text: Did you see the news about the baby whales in Argentina?
Dead calves keep {{washing up}} on beaches in the south of the country. Scientists are {{looking into}} it.
How many are we talking about?
There's no official number yet. But people who live there say they've seen hundreds.
That's so sad. Weren't those whales almost {{wiped out}} once?
Yes, by whalers. But they've been protected since 1935, and they've {{bounced back}}.
So the species was [[back from the brink]]. Why are the calves {{dying off}} now?
The main theory involves gulls. The birds {{go after}} whales when they {{come up}} to breathe.
Don't the adult whales get hurt too?
They've learned to keep their backs underwater. The calves haven't, so they're [[sitting ducks]].
And then the wounds get infected?
That's the idea. Bacteria have already {{turned up}} in some samples. And warmer water may make them too strong for the calves to {{fight off}}.
Wow. Sounds like [[a perfect storm]]. Could people be part of the problem?
Maybe. One researcher said they can't {{rule out}} a human role yet. The teams are in [[a race against time]] to collect samples before the bodies rot.
If this keeps happening, it could really {{set back}} the whales.
Exactly. That's why they want to {{figure out}} the cause.
I hope they do. This feels like [[a wake-up call]].
